title: Como Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Como wells have a 340-foot median depth, 5.0 gpm median yield, and finished costs modeled at $28,100-$46,000.
h1: Como, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land around Como means dealing mostly with fractured mountain bedrock, not a consistent shallow groundwater formation. DWR permit records within 5 miles show a 340-foot median well depth and a 5.0 gpm median pump yield. Those figures are useful for early planning, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce on a particular lot.

This page uses permitted wells near Como, including records from the surrounding Park County area. It covers well depth, water levels, drilling history, likely costs, and the checks that matter before buying or building. Nearby Jefferson, Fairplay, and Hartsel can provide broader context, but the local fractured-bedrock results are the most relevant starting point.

sections.heading: Como well depths reflect fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Como wells have a median reported depth of 340 feet. The middle half runs from 240 to 450 feet, so a driller bidding a normal local well will likely need to allow for a substantial rock hole rather than a shallow installation. A deeper result is possible: the 90th-percentile depth is 550 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,950 feet.

Depths vary considerably from lot to lot because most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. The depth mix shows 53% of wells between 300 and 600 feet, while 36% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 3% are under 100 feet. Ask for a site-specific bid and confirm what casing, grout, access, and extra footage are included.

sections.heading: What a Como well is likely to produce
sections.html:
The reported median pump yield near Como is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.0 and 7.0 gpm. That is a planning range, not a guaranteed flow rate. Nearly half of reported wells, 49%, produce between 5 and 15 gpm, while 41% are in the 1-to-5 gpm range.

Low-yield wells are part of the local risk: 5% report less than 1 gpm, and another 5% report more than 15 gpm. A buyer should evaluate storage capacity and household demand along with the pump test. A well producing slowly may still work for a home if storage and the permitted use fit the property, but a permit and a neighbor’s yield do not establish your lot’s supply.

sections.heading: Water levels in Como need a careful reading
sections.html:
Among the limited records reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 130 feet, with the middle half from 80 to 200 feet. That affects pump selection, electrical planning, and the cost of lifting water to the pressure tank. It also helps explain why a shallow-looking surface location does not necessarily mean a shallow well.

The decade series does not show a simple, steady decline. Median depth to water was 95 feet in the 1970s, 70 feet in the 1980s, 208 feet in the 2000s, 180 feet in the 2010s, and 130 feet in the 2020s. Only 272 records report static water level, so treat this as a record-history signal rather than a site-specific trend prediction.

sections.heading: Como permit history shows long-running local drilling
sections.html:
DWR records contain 2,625 permitted wells within the Como study area. Of those, 1,744 are recorded as constructed, and 1,929 report a total depth. Permitting was active across several decades, with 747 permits in the 2000s, 604 in the 1990s, and 244 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most frequently listed driller is Allen Drilling & Excavating Co., Inc. (Allen, Jack R.), with 811 records. Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert) appears on 173, and Whitewater Drilling Inc. (Benkufski, John D.) on 149. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the written scope before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Como well costs real money
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured granite and gneiss and a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the median depth of 340 feet, the drilled hole models at about $22,100 to $34,000. That is the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

Including a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled finished-well range is about $28,100 to $46,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, or unusual electrical and trenching work can change the bid. Use the 240-to-450-foot local middle range when comparing proposals, and require the contractor to state what happens if the first hole is dry or produces less water than expected.

sections.heading: Como lots need water, environmental, and septic checks
sections.html:
Most permitted wells near Como are for domestic or household use: 94% of the use mix. The records identify 0% Denver Basin aquifer wells and predominantly describe unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 2,469 wells in that category. A household-use permit still has specific conditions, so review the permit with Colorado DWR before assuming future uses are allowed. Exempt household-use wells also have a 35 gpm pumping limit.

Environmental review matters here. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test existing water where available and ask about local site history. Before building, verify well-to-septic separation, septic suitability, driveway access, electric service, and the county building requirements. Fractured rock can also produce low-yield or dry holes.

sections.heading: Buy or build in Como with the well first
sections.html:
Before closing on a lot, obtain the DWR permit number, construction report, pump test, static water level, water-quality results, and any well-use restrictions. Compare nearby records rather than relying on one neighbor. The Como data support planning around a 340-foot median depth, 5.0 gpm median yield, and 130-foot median static water level, but those are area statistics, not a promise for the parcel.

For a new build, have a driller walk the access route and price the complete system, including the pump, tank, trenching, electrical work, casing, and grout. Then coordinate the well location with septic and the house foundation. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask DWR and the county whether an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement applies. A well contingency in the purchase contract is sensible when the site has not yet been drilled.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Como, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Como is 340 feet. The middle half runs from 240 to 450 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 550 feet. Most records are in fractured mountain bedrock, so depth can vary sharply between nearby lots. The deepest recorded well is 1,950 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Como?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at $22,100 to $34,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $28,100 to $46,000. Access, extra depth, casing, grout, and electrical conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Como well produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield near Como is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.0 and 7.0 gpm. Forty-one percent of reported wells produce 1 to 5 gpm, and 5% produce under 1 gpm. A pump test and storage evaluation are more useful for a specific property than the area median alone.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Como?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Como well is safe to drink. Test the actual well for common drinking-water concerns and review local site history. Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental records include 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test again after construction or a change in water quality.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well in Como?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction report, pump test, static water level, water-quality results, and use restrictions. Local records show a 130-foot median static water level and a 5.0 gpm median yield, but individual wells vary. Also confirm septic suitability, well-to-septic separation, access for drilling, electrical service, and whether an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement applies.
